description:
EAT THAI FOOD and DO CHEAP SHOPPING in one of the largest and tallest Chedi in Thailand.
Nakhon Pathom Temple Festival at Wat Phra Pathom Chedi takes place every year for 9 days in December. 

You’ll find many items and souvenirs on sale, from cheap clothes to children’s toys, and phone cases. 

The market is HUGE. The platform on which the stupa sits is a square structure, and the market encompasses all 4 sides of it. In addition to that, there are many twists and turns that branch out from the main area of the market. You will surely get lost if you aren’t paying attention to where you’re going.

And that’s okay because I got lost too.

Nakhon Pathom is about an hour away from Bangkok by car. 

If you don’t have access to your own car you can take a van at BTS Victory Monument which will take you to a nearby Big C grocery store and you’ll have to take another 5 minute motorbike taxi to get to the temple.

I recommend booking a train  from your current destination to Nakhon Pathom as it is the cheapest option and takes roughly the same time as travelling by car (~1 hour).

tags: emsphere|emsphere bangkok|emsphere ikea|emsphere food|em district|Emporium & Emquartier|Emporium|Emquartier|bangkok shopping mall|bangkok mall|mall in bangkok|siam paragon|icon siam|best mall in bangkok|Emsphere bangkok stores|Emsphere bangkok restaurants|luxury mall bangkok|luxuary shopping bangkok|how to get to emsphere|emsphere bangkok food court|central world bangkok|terminal 21|Phrom Phong BTS Station|Emsphere at EM District|bangkok shopping|fft
description:
The Emsphere, the newest shopping mall in Bangkok, is located in the heart of the city, adjacent to BTS Phrom Phong station. It is easily accessible, although the walk from the station may be a bit long. However, the skywalk makes it a breeze.

The lower floors are home to a variety of restaurants, as well as an event space. The restaurants are all quite luxurious and spacious. Upstairs, you'll find fashion, gadgets, and electronics. The interior of the mall is modern and stylish.

The highlight of the mall is the Ikea on the third floor. The store is surprisingly comprehensive, with a wide variety of products. You could easily spend hours browsing the aisles. The Ikea food court is also quite large and inviting.

In addition to the Ikea, the mall also has a showroom for luxury cars and supercars.

The upper floors are reserved for UOB Live, which is not yet open. It is expected to open in early 2024.

Overall, the Emsphere is still under construction. There are still some finishing touches to be done, especially on the ceiling. However, it is already one of the most exciting shopping malls in Bangkok. There are plenty of photo opportunities, and even the bathrooms are stunning.

title: "Day Trip to Koh Kret | Bangkok’s Local Island Adventure!"
tags: Koh Kret|Ko Kret|Koh Kret Thailand|Koh Kret Bangkok|day trip from Bangkok|Bangkok hidden gem|island near Bangkok|pottery village Thailand|things to do in Koh Kret|Koh Kret travel guide|Bangkok day trips|off the beaten path Thailand|local Thai experience|Thai island vlog|Thailand slow life|Thai food tour|Bangkok weekend trip|hidden places in Thailand|cycling in Thailand|Bangkok vlog|bangkok vlog|bangkok 2025|thailand 2025|friendsfromthailand|fft
description:
Koh Kret (or Ko Kret / เกาะเกร็ด) is a charming island in the Chao Phraya River, just north of Bangkok in Nonthaburi Province. It’s perfect for a peaceful half-day or day trip from Bangkok — no beach here, but you’ll find local culture, pottery, food, and slow life vibes. 🌿🚲🍵

Why Visit Koh Kret?
🏺 Pottery Village – Famous for traditional Mon-style pottery. You can watch artisans at work or even try making your own.

🚲 Bike Around the Island – Rent a bicycle and cycle along scenic paths through small villages and riverside homes.

🥢 Local Food – Try rare Mon dishes, giant river prawns, Thai desserts, and more at the weekend market.

🧘‍♀️ Chill, Local Vibes – No cars allowed on the island! It’s a slow-paced, peaceful place.

🛕 Wat Poramaiyikawat – The main temple with a leaning white stupa and a small museum.

🎨 Handicrafts & Souvenirs – Handmade candles, snacks, herbal products, and ceramics.

How to Get to Koh Kret from Bangkok
By Car or Taxi:

Head to Wat Sanam Neua Pier (วัดสนามเหนือ) in Nonthaburi.

Take the short ferry ride (2–5 THB) across the river to Koh Kret.

By Public Transport:

MRT to Nonthaburi Civic Center Station or Pak Kret area

Then grab a taxi or local songthaew to Wat Sanam Neua Pier

By Boat (Fun Option!):

Take the Chao Phraya Express Boat to Pak Kret Pier (N33) (weekend boats only).

Hire a local boat or walk to the ferry pier.

🗓️ Best Time to Visit
Weekends – That’s when the island comes alive with the floating/local market.

Morning – For cooler weather and fewer crowds.

📝 Tips:
Rent a bike for ~40 THB

Wear comfy shoes (some walking or biking involved)

Bring cash (many stalls don’t take cards)

Try the fried flower tempura, herbal drinks, or Thai-style crepes

description:
We crossed the border from Laos into Cambodia and had been warned about the scams that can take place at both immigration offices (by officials). description:
We travelled up to Northern Cebu and spent 5 nights on the TINY island of Malapascua. We fell in love with the natural, unspoilt, magical charm of the island. Although not much infrastructure and limited roads on the island, it’s easy to get around and explore. We spent our days in the sea spotting the famous thresher sharks, laying on the beach, trying delicious Filipino food and playing with the cutest puppies.

Malapascua, Philippines, is a hidden paradise known for its stunning white-sand beaches, crystal-clear waters, and vibrant marine life. Famous for thresher shark diving 🦈, it’s a must-visit for adventure seekers. Enjoy swimming with friendly dogs, breathtaking drone shots, and exploring hidden spots. The island's welcoming locals and serene atmosphere make it perfect for relaxation and exploration.

We were blown away with how friendly everyone on this island was. We felt so safe and loved - same as everywhere we have visited in the Philippines! Some amazing children stopped us from getting lost and directed us to the hidden lighthouse on the north side of the island on our first day which made us feel so welcome straight away. We enjoyed the north beach and finding hidden coves along the coast line. 

Although Malapascua is fairly difficult to get to (5 hour minivan from Cebu City and then a 45 minute ferry from Maya port), it’s definitely worth the trip if you’re looking for somewhere a bit quieter to spend your days relaxing and exploring such a beautiful island. It was one of our favourite destinations whilst island hopping in the Philippines and we definitely recommend adding it to your Philippines travel itinerary!

With so many choices, we had no idea which restaurant to pick! So, we decided to choose a spot based on the number of customers already seated—always a good sign when you’re looking for the best food, right?

We were not disappointed! The Okonomiyaki was absolutely incredible. From the perfectly crispy bottom to the mouth-watering layers of noodles, pork belly, and egg, every bite was better than the last. It was so good, in fact, that we went back the very next day for seconds! Hiroshima’s Okonomiyaki lived up to the hype and then some.

Whether you're a first-time visitor or a seasoned traveler, Hiroshima’s Okonomiyaki is an experience you won’t want to miss. If you're planning a trip to Japan, be sure to add Okonomi-mura to your itinerary. It's a foodie paradise!

We took the train from Osaka to Nara's deer park where the deer are famously known for bowing. There are over 1,000 free-roaming deer here and they are considered messengers of the Gods. Back at Odawara station, we managed to get a partial refund for the 2 day travel pass that we hardly used which was fantastic!

description:
TOKYO DISNEYLAND - A FULL Day Of Fast Passes, Queue Times, Disney Hacks!

We got to Tokyo Disneyland in Japan at 8.30am as the park opens at 9am. We headed straight to the Baymax Happy Ride which was our FAVOURITE and we were so shocked by how many people were on the side dancing to all Baymax's tunes! We hopped on the Star Tours ride before sorting out all of our fast passes and giving you a few tips and hacks on how to get free fast passes and skip all the queues. We managed to do 3 rides each with free fast passes saving us so much time! 

We walked through Cinderella's beautiful castle to the It's a Small World ride as our lunch settled (check out our previous video for EVERYTHING we ate at Disneyland, it will make you hungry!). We looked round the shops and were tempted by all the Baymax and Winnie the Pooh merch. We went on the Monsters Inc ride, Space Mountain (one of our favourites!) and Toy Story Mania in Tomorrowland where Jason absolutely smashed it and beat me by a mile. 

We got front row spaces for the Baymax Cooling Parade where we got absolutely SOAKED whilst dancing to the Happy Ride songs and cooling off in the hot Tokyo heat. We did some of the smaller rides in Adventureland and then queued up for Splash Mountain, our longest wait of the whole day but it was so worth it to get wet and cool down! 

We used our fast passes for the Winnie the Pooh ride  Pooh's Honey Hunt in Fantasyland before getting front row seats for the incredible night parade where we saw Mickey Mouse, the Disney princesses, Toy Story characters and more. On our way out of the park, we managed to get in the queue for the parks NEWEST RIDE Beauty and the Beast and we are so glad we did as it was absolutely incredible and the castle was beautiful, it just had such a long queue all day and you can't get free fast passes for this one. 

We had the BEST day at Tokyo Disneyland and hope you loved the video! If you did, please remember to like it and subscribe to our channel for more.

Tsukiji Fish Market is high on most tourists itineraries when visiting Tokyo, Japan. Before 2018, it was the largest seafood market in the world! In more recent times, it is more of a tourist attraction hotspot than an authentic fish market so we discuss whether we think it is still worth visiting or one to miss, along with the cost of the street food. 

We got ourselves a matcha latte before tasting some grilled tuna skewers with wasabi, despite it being so early in the morning! title: Why We Didn't Try Michelin Star Ramen in Tokyo, Japan!
tags: Places to eat in Tokyo|Tokyo food vlog|Best places to eat in Tokyo|Best ramen in Tokyo|Best ramen shop in Tokyo|Ramen street Tokyo|Michelin star ramen Tokyo|Ramen Tokyo|Food vlog Japan|Amazing food in Tokyo|Is food in Tokyo expensive|Where is the best ramen in Tokyo|Backpacking in Japan|Backpackers in Japan vlog|Traditional Japanese food|Food vlog in Tokyo|Michelin star restaurants in Tokyo|Michelin star food Japan|Michelin star food Tokyo|ramen street
description:
We really wanted to try Tokyo's Michelin Star ramen at Nakiryu. We knew it was going to be busy but we had no idea you had to get a ticket at 8am for the shop opening at 11am so we got there just after 11am and all the tickets were sold out!! So after this failed attempt, we headed to Ramen Street underneath Tokyo Station to get our ramen fix as we didn't have time to go back (this time!). 

Ramen Street has 8 shops all serving... you guessed it, RAMEN! The idea behind the street is to bring together many different types of ramen and every shop puts their own unique spin on their ramen, from different toppings, noodles or sauce - every ramen is different so you never get bored! 

We chose one at random and chose one that specialises in seafood ramen and kelp soy sauce. We had just enough cash to get us two bowls of their standard ramen. We queued up for about 10 minutes outside and then once we were seated, our ramen came out straight away. It was so delicious but sadly not Michelin rated!

description:
Whilst visiting Phong Nha, we HAD to visit The Duck Stop, one of the most popular tourist attractions in the area! This HILARIOUS attraction in Phong Nha is an absolute must do on your Vietnam itinerary and we can see why so many people travel to Phong Nha just to do this! 

We paid 100,000 dong each (approx £3) and this included one soft drink/beer, 20 minutes with the ducks and crispy pancakes, the best food we've had in Vietnam so far. And of course meeting the friendliest Vietnamese people who own the farm and learning all about the crops they grow there. We were absolutely in love with the ducks and had the best experience, we haven't laughed so hard in a long time. You get to feed them, become a 'duck leader', hold one and have a special duck massage which is a feeling that really cannot be explained.

We also learnt so much about Vietnamese culture and traditional farm life; growing rice, fruit trees and why they keep the different animals on the farm. One of these animals was Mr Donald Trump, a 10 year old 700 kilo rescue water buffalo, who you can meet for an extra 50,000 dong (approx £1.50). It was amazing to get so close to him and learn more about these beautiful giants that we see every single day in Vietnam.

At the end of the experience, we were served a traditional Vietnamese crispy pancake (Bánh xèo) wrapped in rice paper and homemade peanut sauce made on the farm. We were taught how to prepare it, eat it and it was SO delicious.

title: Riding the Ho Chi Minh Highway – Phong Nha to Khe Sanh by Motorbike
tags: Vietnam|Vietnamese|Vietnam travel blog|Vietnam travel vlog|Vietnam travel|Vietnam videos|Vietnam travel videos|Vietnam motorcycles|Vietnam Motorbike travel vlog|Motorcycle travel vlog|Motorbike travel vlog Vietnam|Motorbiking through Vietnam|Motorcycle Vietnam travel videos|Backpacker travel vlog|Backpacker in Vietnam|Vietnam backpacking motorcycle vlog|Phong nha|Ho Chi Minh|Ho Chi Minh trail|Beautiful mountain roads Vietnam|Where to motorcycle in Vietnam
description:
We’ve now started our 2 month journey through Vietnam and a whopping 1600km ride, on 2 motorbikes that we purchased in Hanoi. 

We left Phong Nha after staying there for 15 DAYS!! (we originally only intended on staying there for 3 days, but we loved it that much we found it really hard to leave). If you’re including Phong Nha on your Vietnam itinerary, we recommend you add at least 2 days on top of your original plan… it’s great) 

Staying in Phong Nha longer gave us time to relax, visit paradise cave, have our motorbikes serviced, experience Vietnam national day and spend Jason’s birthday in a familiar place. 

We decided to get ourselves (and the motorbikes) off of the infamous QL1 better known as highway 1. If you haven’t driven down it before you’re not missing out on a great deal (in the north especially) it’s a mixture of loud lorries, fast moving buses on a mission & a huge headache.

The road we decided to take was the much more beautiful ‘Ho Chi Minh Trail’ road. This road is not only one of the most beautiful motorbikes drives in Vietnam, it runs really close the Laos border with its many swoops and bends.

The total drive from Phong Nha to Khe Sanh is 233Km which we did over the course of 2 days. The first 99Km drive was to Lon Son, a small town situated in between huge limestone hills/mountain like structures. 

It was a really hot day and we stupidly did not pack enough water, between us we had just over 1.5litres. We expected to see some roadside sellers along the way but after about 1 hour we realised this wasn’t going to happen. We only passed about 10 other people driving this day, which means the road itself isn’t busy enough to be able to warrant people selling food & drink on the roads like we’ve been used to seeing so far. 

We arrived in Lon son at 2.30pm (which made the total drive 4 hours) we had a few stops in between to allow the bikes to cool down and also take in some of the scenery around us. 

We found a place to stay (name of hotel unknown but it was the only place to stay in the area) it cost 300,000 VND / £9 / $12 for a basic but decent hotel room with air-con, hot shower & comfy bed (three things that feel amazing after a days ride).

Jason started his bike to get fuel, and realised his bikes electrics weren’t functioning properly. Luckily in this small town there was a mechanic right next to the hotel, a new battery was fitted & this was completed in 10 minutes costing 400,000 VND / £12 / $16. 

The hotel we stayed in cooked us some rice, vegetables and meat which went down really well alongside some Pringles, sweets & film in bed. 

The next day we set off at 9am, it rained heavily in the night and was lightly raining in the morning BUT this was as good as it was going to get. 
The rain didn’t stop, it was lightly raining for most of the drive (and some parts towards the end VERY heavily) a small incident occurred whilst driving, one of the bungee cords holding Jason’s bag in place suddenly snapped and got trapped in his wheel whilst driving, luckily nothing happened when it did but it could have been a lot worse.

We experienced so many friendly faces on this drive, every time we drove past someone (mainly children) we received either a wave or a huge “HELLOOOOO” and apart from some beautiful waterfalls on the side of the road and driving through thick clouds/fog at the top of a very high mountain where we couldn’t see 10 metres in front of us, not much happened on this drive. We tried to keep our heads down and make it to Khe Sanh safely, which we did at about 3pm. It took us quite a while to do this 134KM drive as the weather was awful and in Jason’s words “the hardest drive I’ve ever done in my life” (this was due to weather not by any means the beautiful scenery and roads) 

This is the 4 episode of our motorbiking journey through the wonderful country of Vietnam and we not only hope to arrive safely in Ho Chi Minh but to experience this beautiful country as much possible and to document it for anyone watching (including our future selves).

If you would like to be kept up to date with our journey please like, subscribe and turn on your video notifications. 

Thank you so much

title: Vietnam's Ancient Capital Has SO Much To Offer!
tags: hue|hue vietnam|hue travel vlog|things to do in hue vietnam|best things to do hue vietnam|imperial city hue vietnam|imperial city|imperial city hue|abandoned|abandoned places|abandoned water park|abandoned water park hue|dragon water park vietnam|vietnam travel|travel vietnam|travel vlog|couples travel|backpacking in vietnam|backpacking vlog|backpacking vlog vietnam|Hue Vietnam|vinh moc tunnels|dmz vietnam|tunnels in vietnam|travel|travel vlogger
description:
We motorbiked from Khe Sanh to Dong Ha specifically to visit the Vinh Moc tunnels in the DMZ, right on the border of North and South Vietnam. We decided to get a taxi there as we were experiencing the tail end of Typhoon Yagi and it was very windy. We were so surprised by how narrow the tunnels were and could not comprehend that approximately 60 families lived in these tunnels during the war; mothers gave birth, children played, and they all sheltered from the bombs raining down on them. The tunnels stretch for about 2km so we explored as much as we could, descending 20m deep to the lowest floor. The tunnels aren't well lit so it got quite difficult to find our way through in the pitch black, but if you just keep walking, you soon find your way out of one of the entrances (usually walking right out onto the huge white stretch of sand). 

The next day, we motorbiked down to Hue where we visited the abandoned waterpark, Hồ Thủy Tiên, about 10km away from Hue. We had to pay 20,000 VND each to enter (Vietnamese locals said it was a cleaning fee) and 10,000 VND to park our motorbike. The lake surrounding the iconic dragon statue has completely dried up now and there was lots of construction going on in the area so it didn't really feel abandoned at all, aside from the graffti covering the buildings, the smashed glass in the old aquarium and the fact that there was only about 5 other people there. We weren't allowed to drive our motorbike around the waterpark as planned and due to the ongoing construction works, we couldn't get to the abandoned slides or theatre either. It was cool to see and explore the dragon building but it wasn't quite what we expected. 

We then visited the Imperial City, the ancient capital of unified Vietnam. It cost 200,000 VND each to enter but this was so worth it to see all the beautiful buildings. We also paid 100,000 VND for a VR (virtual reality) experience where you fly over the ancient city and can see all of the buildings from above. This was fun and we also appreciated the air conditioning in the room! 

Thank you for watching and if you got this far, please like this video and subscribe to our channel for more.

tags: Moto vlog|Motorcycle|Motorbike vlogs|Motorbike Vietnam vlog|Motorcycle Vietnam videos|Motorbike Vietnam vloggers|Travel videos Vietnam|Travel Vietnam by motorcycle|Tourists on motorbike Vietnam|Is Vietnam safe for tourists|Hue Vietnam|Vietnam travel videos|Backpackers in Vietnam|backpacking Vietnam vlog|Vietnam travel itinerary|Vietnam number 1|Motorcycle vlog|Vietnam travel vlog|Hue travel itinerary|Things to see in Hue
description:
Our 2-month journey through Vietnam continues with a massive 1600km ride, all the way from Hanoi to Hue, on two motorbikes we bought in Hanoi. After two successful days riding along the iconic Ho Chi Minh Highway, we arrived in Khe Sanh—a stopover on our journey that didn’t hold much for us apart from the Khe Sanh Museum. We only stayed one night before setting our sights on Hue.

Before leaving, we took a break in a local coffee shop, discussing our route for the day as a typhoon was heading toward the north. We could already feel the effects of the strong winds in Khe Sanh, and we knew it was important to plan our route carefully for safety.

With coffee in hand and water bottles fueling us up, we headed south toward Dong Ha. But just 5 minutes into our ride, Erin noticed a flat tyre, so we stopped by a friendly local mechanic for a quick fix. With the wind picking up and light rain falling, the ride to Dong Ha was a bit challenging, and we missed the calmness of the Ho Chi Minh Trail.

We arrived in Dong Ha around 1pm and treated ourselves to a little comfort at the Saigon Hotel, costing just £10 each for a spacious and luxurious room. After checking in, we quickly booked a taxi to the Vinh Moc Tunnels—a decision we were glad we made as the wind was even stronger. The taxi ride was £18 for a return trip, a small price to pay for comfort after a rough couple of days.

If you want to learn more about the Vinh Moc Tunnels, make sure to check out our Hue Vlog for the full experience.

The next morning, after the winds calmed slightly, we set off for Hue on our motorbikes. Along the way, we were passed by 20-25 green army trucks, likely returning from supporting Hanoi during Typhoon Yagi.

We arrived in Hue at around 2pm, and immediately felt the pulse of the city. Traffic in Hue was hectic, especially around the bridges, but our backpacks tied to our bikes gave the locals an indication that we were new to the area, and they gave us the space we needed.

While this ride wasn’t as scenic as our time on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, it led us toward more incredible roads, including the legendary Hai Van Pass, which will be the highlight of our next adventure. Stay tuned for more as we continue our journey through Vietnam on motorbikes! 🏍️

Join us on an unforgettable one-day backpacking adventure in Hoi An, Vietnam! 

Hoi An, Vietnam is a charming UNESCO World Heritage town famous for its beautifully preserved Ancient Town. The narrow streets are lined with colorful lanterns, and riverside cafes offer some of the best street food in Vietnam. Hoi An is also renowned for its tailor shops, where visitors can get custom-made clothes, from dresses to suits, often completed in just 24 hours. The town is a hub for unique cultural experiences, such as basket boat tours through lush coconut forests and hands-on cooking classes that teach traditional Vietnamese dishes. With its rich history, vibrant culture, and mouthwatering street food scene, Hoi An is a must-visit destination for travelers in Vietnam.

Our day begins with a British breakfast of Heinz beans on toast, after stocking up on UK and Australian food at a local deli. Then, we hop on our motorbikes and head to the famous Coconut Village, where we embark on an amazing basket boat tour through the lush coconut forest. At just 180,000 VND (approx £5), the tour is an incredible value, and we even capture some stunning drone shots of the scenic river!

After the boat tour, we stop by a local mechanic in Hoi An for a quick motorbike service to prepare for our upcoming Vietnam backpacking journey to Ho Chi Minh City. Next, we visit the charming Hoi An Ancient Town and pick up our tailor-made clothes—Erin gets a beautiful dress for £40, and Jason picks up a stylish linen shirt for £25. title: Accidentally Crossing the BORDER From Vietnam to Laos!
tags: Vietnam|Vietnam travel videos|Vietnam travel|Vietnam travel vlog|Motovlog|Motorcycle vlog|Motorbike vlog|Laos|Cambodia|Backpacker|Backpacker in Vietnam|Backpacking Vietnam|Travel|Travelling|South east Asia|South east Asia travel|Border crossing|Border crossing Vietnam|Travel advice south east Asia|border crossing|border crossing gone wrong|vietnam to laos border crossing|denied entry into vietnam|vietnam police|vietnamese police|border crossing scam|scam
description:
🌍 Want to visit the Indochina T Junction? Don’t make the same mistake we did! It’s a beautiful, historic location but make sure you have the right maps and check your border crossings carefully.

💬 Have you ever had a travel mishap like this? Share your story in the comments below!

👍 If you enjoyed this video, don’t forget to like, comment, and subscribe for more crazy travel stories and tips!

We wanted to visit the Indochina T Junction while staying the night in Plei Kan. The Indochina T Junction is the point where Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia meet, marked by a monument symbolising the friendship between the three countries. It’s a unique border crossing location, offering a rare glimpse into the region’s cultural unity and there is a statue you can visit. However, after putting the wrong location into our offline maps, we ended up at the Laos-Vietnam border instead. We had absolutely no idea that, as we approached, and the immigration officer waved us through, we had actually left Vietnam.

We drove around ‘no man’s land’ for a while, even buying a soft drink from a Laos shop, until we reached the entrance of Laos, where the guard told us to stop and asked for our passports. We quickly realised our mistake and drove back to the entrance into Vietnam. However, this is where things took a turn for the worse...

The guard who initially waved us through the Vietnam gate came over, shouting at us, saying he told us to stop and demanding to see our passports. This did not happen, but unfortunately, we didn’t catch it on camera, so we can’t prove anything (other than the fact that no one shouted after us or came after us on bikes once we had gone through the gate). We were denied entrance into Vietnam for about 5 minutes and couldn’t easily explain our mistake due to a huge language barrier... and a huge physical barrier blocking us from coming back in!

Eventually, there was no other option but for them to let us through, as we could not communicate, and we think it was pretty obvious we hadn’t entered Laos as we were only 5 minutes away and had one small bag with us. The whole experience was quite scary, and after reading reviews of the Vietnam Laos border crossing online, we realise how lucky we were to get back through without having to pay anything!

title: Lo Xo Pass by Motorbike – One of Vietnam’s Best Mountain Roads

description:
Motorbiking Through Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh Road: Lo Xo Pass, Indochina Junction, & Unexpected Border Crossing!

🌍 Join us as we journey from Hoi An to Kham Duc, Plei Kan, Pleiku, and beyond, exploring the stunning countryside, rural Vietnam, and experiencing unexpected challenges, all while learning about the culture and history along the way.

🚴‍♀️ What is it REALLY like to motorbike through Vietnam’s rugged backroads? We travel off-the-beaten-path, from the Lo Xo Pass to the serene Sea Lake near Pleiku, sharing the highs and lows of the ride.

Leaving Hoi An felt chaotic. We hadn’t been on the bikes for a while, so we were a bit rusty. The traffic was dense, and it took a while to get used to the flow again. Once we hit the quieter roads, it was a relief, and the ride became much smoother. Our destination that day was Kham Duc, 111km west of Hoi An.

We made a quick detour to My Son Sanctuary, a collection of Hindu temples built between the 4th and 13th centuries by the Champa kings. The site, though partially in ruins, was still a fascinating glimpse into Vietnam’s ancient past. We’ve got a full video about My Son on our channel – be sure to check it out!

After exploring the temples, we were back on the road toward Kham Duc. The rain started pouring again, and the ride became even tougher. Our bodies were not used to long rides, so every bump on the road felt brutal! But as we drove deeper into rural Vietnam, the landscape grew more beautiful, and the sight of smiling locals made the struggle worth it.

We arrived in Kham Duc and checked into the cozy 21 Guesthouse and Yoga. The owner was incredibly friendly and gave us great tips for local food and things to do. After drying off our clothes, we indulged in a warm meal of Bánh xèo and hit the hay for a much-needed rest.

The next morning, we were off to Plei Kan, 110km away. We were excited to see the Lo Xo Pass – though we didn’t quite know what to expect! We left the guesthouse, only for Erin to discover she had a flat tire. Fortunately, a mechanic nearby fixed it for just 30,000 VND (about £1).

As we continued, the roads became a challenge. For two hours, we encountered cracked concrete roads, roadworks, and aggressive trucks honking and driving too close. We had to stay alert the entire time, which meant we didn’t get a chance to enjoy the Lo Xo Pass – and only realized we’d passed through it much later!

We arrived in Plei Kan around 2pm, dropped our bags at the hotel, and set out again to see the Indochina Junction, a monument where the borders of Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos meet. But things took a wild turn when we accidentally crossed into Laos! We had trouble getting back into Vietnam, and it became quite an ordeal. We’ve made a separate video about this crazy experience – stay tuned for that!

Next, we visited the famous Sea Lake (Bien Ho), a large freshwater lake near Pleiku. It’s known for its “sea-like” waves during the rainy season, making it a must-see. Since we were in coffee plantation territory, we decided to visit a local coffee farm. Erin had found one with an adjoining café, so we took a Grab taxi. However, the driver abandoned us halfway down a dirt track because the road was so bad. The café was closed, and we were stranded with no Wi-Fi. 

We hiked back to the nearest town and managed to call a taxi back to Pleiku. Exhausted and frustrated, we grabbed some pizza and crashed for the night, ready for the next day’s adventure.

This is the 7th episode of our motorbiking journey through Vietnam. We hope to make it safely to Ho Chi Minh City while experiencing as much of the country as possible and documenting it for our future selves and all of you watching!

description:
Buying our own motorbikes in Hanoi and riding all the way down to Ho Chi Minh City has given us the freedom to explore off-the-beaten-path destinations in Vietnam. After leaving Hoi An, we made our way to My Son Sanctuary, a UNESCO World Heritage site in central Vietnam, home to ancient Hindu temples built by the Champa Kingdom between the 4th and 13th centuries. The site offers rich history, stunning architecture, and breathtaking scenery. Though many of the temples were destroyed in the war, we enjoyed exploring the site and could have spent much more time there if we didn’t have 110km to cover.

Arriving in Kham Duc, we rested before starting our day with an incredibly cheap iced coffee. Kham Duc is a small town in central Vietnam, located along the historic Ho Chi Minh Road. Surrounded by lush mountains and dense forests, it offers a peaceful escape with traditional food, waterfalls, and local culture. During the Vietnam War, Kham Duc was strategically important, with the U.S. establishing a military base here. Today, it remains a quiet, off-the-beaten-path destination, where travelers can learn about its history, enjoy rural landscapes, and experience local life. Its relaxed atmosphere and proximity to the Vietnam War history make it a unique stop on any journey through central Vietnam.

Jason spotted a nearby waterfall on his map, and with the help of two friendly local boys, we found it! Our Vietnamese isn’t great, but we managed to eat a delicious chicken noodle soup with peanuts and mild chili sauce—simple, but tasty. 

We also joined a local yoga class at our homestay and later indulged in beef noodles and Bánh xèo (Vietnamese crispy pancake), both of which were incredible. Bánh xèo (one of our favourite dishes) s a Vietnamese crispy pancake made from rice flour, turmeric, and coconut milk. It’s typically filled with shrimp, pork, bean sprouts, and herbs, then folded and served with fresh greens and a tangy dipping sauce. A delicious street food! The food, the culture, and the people of Kham Duc made it the perfect stop on our journey along the Ho Chi Minh road.

description:
In this travel vlog, we explore the quirky mountain town of Da Lat in Vietnam, a place with over 1,000 hotels but not much to do—at least, that’s what we thought! After a long motorbike ride through the bustling streets of Vietnam, we finally arrived in Da Lat, expecting a serene escape into the mountains. 

However, what we found was a town with a strange abundance of hotels, most of which seemed almost empty or had just a few rooms occupied. It left us scratching our heads—why are there so many hotels in a town that feels relatively quiet and less touristy than other spots in Vietnam?

Located 1,500 meters above sea level, Da Lat offers a cooler climate compared to the rest of Vietnam, making it a popular retreat from the heat of the lowlands. The temperature is much cooler, often requiring only a light jacket, and the town doesn't even need air conditioning or fans in most hotels. 

The cool climate and stunning mountainous landscapes make it an ideal spot for locals seeking a weekend getaway and for a few international travelers looking to enjoy some peace and tranquility. Da Lat is also known for its French colonial architecture, charming cafes, and scenic views of lakes and forests, which provide a peaceful atmosphere perfect for unwinding.

Despite the town’s low-key vibe, Da Lat still manages to have some fun attractions. We decided to check out the alpine coaster, one of the town's main highlights. The coaster takes you on a thrilling 20-minute ride down the mountainside to Datanla Waterfall, one of the area's most famous natural sights. It was an exciting experience, and we couldn’t resist buying a ride photo as a memento of the adventure! It costs 250,000 VND each (£7.70) but we got sucked into buying the ride photo at a cost of 90,000 VND (£2.70) as well. 

After the ride, we stopped by Goc Ha Thanh, a local restaurant, to try wonton soup—our first time tasting this delicious dish, and it certainly didn’t disappoint. Of course, we also got caught in the rain while wandering around, but it didn’t stop us from exploring the area.

As we spent more time in Da Lat, we couldn’t help but wonder why there are so many hotels in a place that seems so quiet and peaceful, with fewer attractions than other tourist-heavy areas in Vietnam. In this episode of our Vietnam Motorbike Diaries, we leave the cool, misty mountains of Da Lat and head towards the sunny coast of Mui Ne. Our journey takes us through one of the most iconic mountain roads in southern Vietnam—the Ngoạn Mục Pass (Sông Pha Pass)—known for its steep slopes and breathtaking views. 

With a descent of 700m, we navigate sharp bends while flying a drone to capture the stunning scenery from above. Along the way, we also pass Vietnam’s first hydroelectric power station and drive beneath massive hydraulic water pipes suspended over the mountain.

After conquering the pass, we stop for a roadside pho before heading to Mui Dinh, a quiet beach town where we spend the night listening to the calming sound of waves crashing from our simple but charming hotel for just £9.

The next day, we continue our journey along the QL1 highway, driving past dusty mountain landscapes until the incredible Mui Ne sand dunes come into view, accompanied by the sight of vibrant jeeps on sunset tours. After checking into our accommodation, May Bungalow, with a gorgeous pool, we unwind at the Pineapple Beach Bar where we enjoy cold beers while watching local fishermen cast their nets at sunset.

description:
Add Mui Ne To Your Vietnam Itinerary! 

After nearly three months of traveling through Vietnam, we’ve finally arrived at one of the country’s most iconic destinations—the stunning sand dunes of Mui Ne! 🌵 Located on Vietnam’s south coast, about 200km from Ho Chi Minh City, Mui Ne feels like a desert oasis right out of the Sahara. In this episode, we take a break from our motorbikes and book a jeep tour to explore the colorful dunes and nearby attractions.

We started our afternoon jeep tour at 1:30pm with a visit to the Fairy Stream and the bustling Fishing Village before heading off to the famous Mui Ne Sand Dunes. The dunes themselves are not only incredibly beautiful but also a lot of fun! Whether you’re into dune bashing or simply soaking up the views, there’s something magical about this desert landscape. 🏜️

For a truly unforgettable experience, we recommend booking your jeep tour through May Bungalow, a lovely hotel offering affordable luxury right by the beach. It’s the perfect place to relax after your dune adventure, and we can’t recommend it enough! 🏨

When we arrived at the white sand dunes we were greeted by some friendly Quad-bike drivers who have the set price of:

Option 1 
300,000 VND per person ($12) for a fun drive up to the sand dunes, over to the lake and back to the entrance. You get to stay at each place for as long as you want. 
Option 2 
800,000VND ($32) for 1 Quad-bike that you get to drive yourself BUT you have to be back at the entrance within 20 minutes. 

We thought about this for a few minutes before going for option 1 and we’re very glad we did as we got to spend more time at each place.  Join us as we take you through the best parts of Mui Ne, from its vibrant dunes to the peaceful Fairy Stream, and find out why this place is one of the top destinations in Vietnam!

Mui Ne is a cool town with nice bars, restaurants and things to do. You should definitely consider adding it to your itinerary either before or after Ho Chi Minh (depending on which way you’re travelling!). We stayed for 4 nights but if you’re tight on time, 2 nights could also work well.

title: Riding a Motorbike from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City – We Made It
tags: Vietnam|vietnam motorbike vlog|vietnam motorbike|places to ride motorbikes in Vietnam|top gear|top gear route Vietnam|Jeremy Clarkson|James may|the top gear route on motorbikes|travel|travel vlog|travel videos Vietnam|backpacking Vietnam|backpacker vlog|backpacking vietnam|south east Asia|south east asia travel vlog|moto vlog|motorbike vlog|motorbike trips|beautiful motorbike roads|motorbike vietnam|moto|vlog|travelling|travelvlog
description:
Motorbiking Vietnam for the last 2 months has been beautiful, scary, painful and so worth it. 

As we leave Mui Ne in the direction of our last stop, we both individually reflect on what the journey has meant to us. We give our motorbikes a good clean at our accommodation so they’re ready for the last ride and to be sold when we arrive in Ho Chi Minh City. 

The road leading to Ho Chi Minh was mundane, grey and BUSY. It felt like the whole of Vietnam were filtering their way towards the city on the same day as us.

Every kilometre close we got, it got 5% busier. It was so important to stay switched on so we didn’t fall (quite literally) at the last hurdle. 

The sky ahead was grey, like REALLY dark. A storm was brewing and we had 50km to go. As the rain started to splash on our helmets, we knew we were in trouble. We had never experienced rain quite like it. It was aggressive rain, the roads became flooded in ankle deep water within 30 minutes. We had to make a very quick decision to carry on or pull over and we chose to carry on, we were nearly there (we know 50km isn’t close but when we were looking at it from a “let’s finish this 2200km journey” it felt pretty close) 

Most motorbike drivers had pulled over taking shelter under bridges , lorries were whizzing past us and splashing us heavily as they did so. It was intense. Our camera equipment stopped working and our phones were barely hanging on… but eventually we made it to the comfort of Meander Hotel Saigon. 

With the entire contents of our backpacks completely soaked, it wasn’t the end we had in our mind but it was our end and we loved every minute of it. 

This was the last episode of our motorcycle diaries through Vietnam. We hope we have managed to entertain, educate or even inspire you. 

Thank you for watching, our trip in Vietnam has come to an end but we continue our journey on and we hope you are along for the ride too.

Erin & Jason

title: Where To Start a Backpacking Trip In South East Asia?
tags: Backpacking|Backpacker|Thailand|Malaysia|Langkawi|Travel|Travel vlog|Travel advice|Travel videos|Backpacking advice|South east Asia|South east Asia travel vlog
description:
So you’ve made the decision to backpack around south east Asia, but the next question is, where do you start?
People for many years have started their backpacking trips in Bangkok. More specifically Ko Sann Road. This is a fantastic place for any backpacker to start and has it all. But just because people for years have started there doesn’t mean you have to.

Langkawi, an archipelago of 99 islands off the coast of Malaysia, is a tropical paradise that offers backpackers a perfect blend of adventure, nature, and relaxation. Known for its stunning beaches, lush rainforests, and vibrant nightlife, Langkawi is an ideal destination for those looking to unwind or explore.
For beach lovers, Pantai Cenang is the main hub, with its lively atmosphere, budget accommodations, and array of bars and restaurants. If you prefer something quieter, head to the more tranquil beaches like Tanjung Rhu or Pantai Tengah. Nature enthusiasts will appreciate Langkawi’s UNESCO Global Geopark, where you can hike through rainforests, visit stunning waterfalls like Telaga Tujuh, and explore the mangroves by kayak or boat.

A must-do is the Langkawi Sky Bridge, an impressive curved suspension bridge offering breathtaking views of the surrounding islands. You can also take the cable car to the top of Gunung Mat Cincang for panoramic vistas of the island and its surrounding waters. For a bit of wildlife, the Langkawi Wildlife Park and Underwater World offer encounters with exotic creatures.
Despite its growing popularity, Langkawi still maintains a laid-back vibe that’s perfect for backpackers on a budget. Affordable hostels, guesthouses, and street food stalls abound, making it easy to keep costs low while enjoying all that the island has to offer. Whether you’re seeking adventure or simply a place to relax, Langkawi provides the perfect escape.

description:
We visited a children's charity in Manila, Children of the Dump, part of the Asian Student Christian Trust. This charity supports children and families who are living and working on Manila’s largest rubbish dump, a place where nobody should have to live. These families are living in incredibly difficult conditions and the children are fighting hard to have an education. This would be  impossible without the support of the Asian Student Christian Trust so we have made this video to help raise awareness and show the incredible work being done to give these children a chance at a better life.

💔 Philippines… these children need our help!

We visited the rubbish dump to see the heartbreaking situation for ourselves. Families are living alongside flies, rats and rubbish in a smelly and unclean environment. They live here because the parents work as scavengers, collecting plastic and metal from the rubbish dump and selling it to junk shops for a very small wage. Their houses are made from any materials they can scavenge and in some houses, there are 6 people sharing one bed. They do not have access to electricity or running water. Sometimes, children will help their parents scavenge on the rubbish dump instead of attending school because surviving has to come first. Their living situation is heartbreaking but we are determined to help. 

🤝 The Charity 

The charity ‘Children of the Dump’, part of the Asian Student Christian Trust, supports these families in many different ways. They run a free school which is located at the rubbish dump, which avoids any transport costs and means the children are put into education at a very early age. They also run free classes at the charity centre for over 140 children in the wider community, allowing them to further their education outside of public school, teaching a wide variety of classes from leadership, teamwork and dance. Of course these classes are not free to run and are solely reliant on donations from the public. 

The charity also provides a monthly supplement to some of the families living on the dump, helping with food and transport costs. The work this charity does is quite simply life changing. It’s a tough reality, but we want to shed light on the incredible work being done to help these children and provide them with a better future. The charity staff are so passionate about the work they do and are kind, caring and supportive people. In this video, we asked some of the staff to explain the work that the charity does and how it actually helps the community so you can hear it firsthand.

description:
The weekend is here, which means we finally get to visit the Salcedo Morning Market. This famous market in Manila is a vibrant weekend destination offering a wide variety of fresh produce, local delicacies, organic goods, and handmade crafts. Located in Salcedo Village, Makati, it attracts locals and tourists alike with its lively atmosphere and diverse selection of high-quality food and artisanal products. It is open every Saturday from 7:00 AM to 2:00 PM.

We first heard about this from watching Dale Phillips’ vlog in Manila and have always wanted to go, but our timings never matched up. We started off by taking a Grab to the area (it wasn’t far to walk, but we didn’t want to get too sweaty before breakfast). We explored the amazing market for around 15 minutes, building up an appetite and deciding what we wanted to eat. 

After looping through the whole market, Jason spotted one of his favorite coffee shops, Tim Hortons. We’ve only ever had one coffee from there, called French Vanilla. It’s simply the best, and you must try it if you ever pass one. We enjoyed a coffee there, then headed off to get some delicious Hungarian sausage—it was incredibly juicy and tasty.

Next, we tried some empanadas (savory pastries filled with meat, vegetables, or cheese, then deep-fried or baked). There is a stand that offers a really well-priced meal of chorizo silog, which Jason enjoyed while Erin got herself a refreshing cucumber juice. The food was really fresh. The prices were a little high, but that was to be expected for the area and the quality of what we were eating. If you're in Manila on a Saturday, we highly recommend this as both a meal and an experience.

description:
After flying in from Manila, we decided to spend one night and one full day in Puerto Princesa, Palawan's largest city. We wanted to see for ourselves if it’s just a layover city or if it’s worth a stop!

Our first stop was Baywalk, a very popular spot in Puerto Princesa, especially on weekends. It was buzzing with families enjoying the evening, with lots of food stalls and entertainment. We could see why it’s such a favourite hangout! We decided to sit at a restaurant for a drink, but things took a scary turn when a lorry crashed into the electric pole right outside, cutting the power and causing a bit of chaos. We cut our evening short but were ready early the next morning to continue exploring.

Next, we walked down to Plaza Quartel, a historical site where 150 American soldiers were imprisoned by the Japanese during World War II. Although it’s meant to be a peaceful park commemorating the fallen, it’s currently undergoing a 15 million peso rehabilitation programme, so there wasn’t much to see, and the area was mostly under construction. Nonetheless, it was still nice to visit and pay our respects.

With the rain starting to pour, we sought shelter back at our hotel while we waited for our 6-hour minivan journey up to El Nido.

Whether you're an adventure seeker, a beach lover, or simply looking to escape into nature, El Nido has something for everyone.

We began our trip here after a very tough drive from Puerto Princesa. We had no idea the roads would be so winding, and just one hour into this six-hour journey, I (Jason) started to feel very unwell. After we checked into our accommodation at OUTPOST HOSTEL, we pretty much just went straight to sleep, as the long drive had drained the life out of us.

On the first morning, still not feeling 100%, we headed into town. The fare for the trike ride was a flat rate of ₱100. We explored the town for a little while and noticed just how much construction was underway. Every building that wasn’t open was being renovated, and the streets had been torn up by diggers.

We wandered around for a couple of hours, saying hello to the friendly locals and stopping off at El Nido Bakery, which seemed to be very popular. While deciding what sweet treats to try, a young boy told us to avoid one of the cakes, as he had eaten it before and said it was (in his words) “very bad.” We think it was because the cake looked really appealing, with bright colors, but when he tasted it, he realized it wasn't fruity but rather just food coloring with unusual flavors. From that moment on, he vowed never to let anyone else make the same mistake.

We were then advised to try one of the donuts, filled with one of the Philippines' favorite ingredients—yes, you guessed it, Ube.

Ube (for those of you who don’t know) is a type of purple yam commonly used in Filipino cuisine. It's known for its striking, vibrant purple color and naturally sweet, nutty flavor. Ube is often used in desserts, such as ube halaya (a sweet, creamy jam-like treat), ube ice cream, and ube cake. Beyond its unique taste, it's prized for its versatility in both traditional and modern dishes. It can be boiled, mashed, or pureed, and its sweet, earthy flavor lends itself to a variety of sweet and savory applications. Ube has recently gained popularity worldwide, especially in fusion desserts and baked goods.

Our total came to only ₱25 ($0.40), which was an amazing deal for some fresh Filipino treats.

description:
Whilst in Cebu during our first-ever visit to the Philippines in May 2024, we noticed just how many Don Macchiatos there were. We had never seen the shop before, either outside of the Philippines or even in Manila. But in Cebu, they are absolutely everywhere.

After a little Google research, we found out that there are over 700 branches in the Philippines, and that it is the cheapest coffee chain in the country. We went for the famous caramel macchiato (both iced and hot), and it did not disappoint. For ₽39, we’d choose this over Starbucks any day!

description:
Are you ready for the ultimate Jollibee challenge? In this vlog, we take on a Jollibee 24-hour fast food challenge, where we eat nothing but Jollibee for an entire day! From breakfast to dinner, we'll be indulging in all of Jollibee's iconic menu items to see if we can survive a full day of Filipino fast food goodness.

Jollibee is the Philippines' most beloved fast food chain, renowned for its unique fusion of American fast food and Filipino flavors. Whether you're craving crispy fried chicken, sweet spaghetti, or juicy burgers, Jollibee offers a wide variety of delicious dishes that cater to all tastes.

We headed down to Makati Avenue bright and early, making sure we were there before the breakfast menu ended at 10am. Jason went for the very traditional Filipino breakfast, cornsilog, while Erin opted for pancakes and maple syrup. We both enjoyed breakfast and were feeling positive about the day ahead.

As lunchtime rolled around, we went back to the Makati Avenue store and ordered our lunch. Jason had wanted to try the Aloha Burger for a long time, ever since he first saw it on the menu months ago. However, it was always out of stock when he went to try it. FINALLY, the stars aligned, and on a beautiful sunny day, he got to try the Aloha Burger.

It was one of our favorite things we've tried from Jellibee and tasted very similar to burgers from McDonald's. Erin went for the Chicken Crunch Burger and fries, which wasn't her favorite, especially compared to the Aloha Burger! We also got some chicken nuggets, purely because we wanted to try the ranch dip-something else that was always out of stock when we visited Jollibee.

The day flew by, and by the time we were ready for dinner, it was pretty late, and neither of us felt like venturing out to the Jollibee store. Luckily, Grab saved the day, and we ordered dinner through the app. Jason chose the Burger Steaks with rice and gravy, one of Jollikee's most famous menu items, while Erin went for her all-time favorite, Jollibee Spaghetti.

We both felt slightly sluggish after a full day of eating fast food, but the wide variety on the Jollibee menu made it a fairly easy challenge, and neither of us got bored with the options.

description:
Manila has almost become like a second home to us while traveling. The city has so many different parts: culture, crazy traffic, great food, high-rise buildings that tower over small, low-rise yet built-up communities, shopping malls, street food—you name it, and Manila has not only got it but they’ve got the best of it.

We’ve grown to love this city for many reasons. We’ve found our favorite spots and have started to return to them time and again, like our favorite breakfast spot, Kanto Freestyle, where we enjoyed some amazing spam and corned beef silog.

I (Jason) had to find a good place to get my haircut now that we’ve been in Manila for a while. When we return in the future, I’ll have a good barber to come back to. I found somewhere online that looked pretty cool and had great reviews. It was a little more expensive compared to other barbershops I had seen, but being a barber myself back in the UK, I don’t mind paying a bit more because I know where that extra money goes. Some people think, “A haircut is just a haircut” and ask, “Why pay more when you can get it for less?” But I know that more money usually means more experience. In the barbering world, unless you own your own shop, there tends to be very little room for development or moving up in management like in other industries. What you can do is work at a shop that pays its staff more, but that usually means they charge more for their haircuts, which in turn reflects higher standards of work. I know this seems obvious, but not everyone understands it... Anyway, I’m rambling.

The place I found did an amazing haircut for ₱350, and it was in a really friendly neighborhood of Manila. When we had a chance to walk around afterward, we were greeted with friendly faces and the famous Filipino hospitality.

description:
Our very first time visiting the Venice Grand Canal Mall in Manila! We had wanted to visit this mall for a really long time so we eventually decided to make the 8km journey from Makati... or 1 hour in traffic!

Venice Grand Canal Mall in Taguig is a stunning shopping and leisure destination inspired by Venice, Italy. The mall features a picturesque canal with gondola rides, creating a romantic atmosphere. Its European-inspired architecture, combined with modern amenities, makes it a popular spot for both locals and tourists.

We really enjoyed people watching by the canal and taking in the beauty of this mall, it's like no other mall we have ever visited before and definitely now one of our favourites. The gondola rides are 500 pesos per person (about £7) so we skipped that this time but we will go back soon to try it out. There is a beautiful padlock love bridge where couples and families secure their own padlock to the bridge as a sign of eternal love, it was so nice to walk along and read all the names written on the padlocks.

We also found a supermarket inside called 'Marketplace' and we both LOVE looking round supermarkets in different countries to see what they have for sale and the difference between the UK.
We actually found lots of UK products in the supermarket as they are a huge import of Waitrose, a premium supermarket we have back in the UK.

description:
During our first visit to the Philippines in May 2024, we were fascinated by the large steel buses we saw everywhere (we later found out they were called "jeepneys").

Now that we know what they are, for those of you who don't, a jeepney is a colorful and iconic Filipino public transport vehicle, known for its unique design and vibrant artwork. It's a cost-effective, open-air ride that can carry many passengers, often customized with local flair. Popular in the Philippines, jeepneys are a symbol of the country’s culture and heritage. They’re big, loud, and look SO cool.

We didn’t get a chance to ride one during our first visit, but we vowed that when we came back, we would get on one. One afternoon in Manila, with not much to do, we decided that today would be the day to finally hop on a jeepney. We stood around for a while, almost stalling. When we finally plucked up the courage, we were greeted by smiling Filipino faces who were more than happy to help and even taught us the phrase “bayad po.”

description:
Halo-halo is a popular Filipino dessert made from a mix of shaved ice, sweetened fruits (like jackfruit and banana), jellies, and beans, topped with leche flan, purple yam (ube), and a scoop of ice cream. It's a refreshing, colorful treat perfect for hot weather and festive occasions.

When we first came to the Philippines in 2024, we wanted to try this dessert, not only because everyone we spoke to said that we had to try it, but mainly because it sounded so crazy and different from the desserts we have back in the UK (the closest thing we could think of was a "Knickerbocker Glory." If you don't know what that is, just give it a Google, haha).
When we tried Halo Halo for the first time, we didn’t realize it, but we made a huge mistake… we forgot to mix the ingredients together and instead ate it layer by layer. For those of you who don’t know (like we didn’t), Halo Halo means "Mix Mix," so when we forgot to mix the ingredients, it was pretty funny for anyone watching who knew what we were doing wrong.
This is our first time in the Philippines, and we’re going to redeem ourselves. It was a hot day in Manila, and we could hear Halo Halo calling our names. It was the middle of the day, we skipped lunch, and went straight to dessert (it’s great being an adult).
As soon as the dish hit the table, we mixed that baby up and dug in. It was so much better than the first time we had it… probably because we mixed it!

description:
We set ourselves the challenge of ONLY eating street food for 24 hours in Manila, just for fun—and we didn’t expect it to open our minds (and taste buds!) to such an incredible variety of flavours. Some of the tastiest food we've had in the Philippines came from street vendors, and we discovered just how safe and delicious it can be. Many tourists are wary of street food, associating it with food poisoning or poor hygiene, but we’re here to debunk that myth. In fact, you’re just as likely to get food poisoning from eating in a restaurant, and by avoiding street food, you’re missing out on so many budget-friendly, mouth-watering options.

We started the day at Salcedo Morning Market (we filmed a separate video on this market, so make sure to check that out too!), where we sampled a fantastic range of both Filipino and international foods. The weekend vibe was amazing, and we tried Hungarian sausage, empanadas, Filipino favourite chorizo pudpud, and fresh fruit juices. By mid-afternoon, we were still full, so we decided to find a light lunch or snack.

On the streets, we came across a stall serving cheesy bibingka, a delicious Filipino delicacy freshly cooked on coals. It was the perfect snack! We also grabbed some chilli and garlic peanuts to nibble on.

For dinner, we enjoyed a sizzling feast of pork skewers, another Hungarian sausage in a bun, and a Mexican birria taco—crispy and filled with marinated meat. As we sat on the street chatting about our love for street food, we got the chance to interact with some locals who were also grabbing their evening meals.

To finish our 24-hour street food adventure, we headed to Legazpi Sunday Market in Makati, where we had a final round of pork sisig, Korean dumplings, and sticky orange chicken with rice—all for a very reasonable price.

We absolutely loved doing this challenge, and it has definitely made us eager to try more! If you’ve made it this far, let us know in the comments what other food challenges you'd like us to take on. We’re ready for the next one!

title: Cheap Sisig vs Expensive Sisig in the Philippines 🇵🇭
tags: The Philippines|Philippines|filipino|filipino vlog|philippines Vlog|Travel vlog|travel vlog philippines|British Vloggers In The Philippines|Backpacker|Backpacker in The Philippines|Travel Vlog South East Asia|South East Asia Travel Videos|Travel Videos|Backpacking Vlog|Travel|Where to go backpacking in south east Asia|Is the Philippines safe|bloggers in the philippines|vloggers in the philippines|filipino food|filipino food vlog|filipino foodie|foodie|manila
description:
Filipino food is amazing, and Manila is a great place to eat it, with so many choices due to the vast number of restaurants. However, trying to find the best place can be tough. In this video, we are on the hunt for the best Sisig in Manila!

After a bit of research on Google and asking a few locals where their favorite place to eat Sisig was, we narrowed it down to the infamous “Aristocrat” Restaurant. It offers a blend of traditional and contemporary Filipino cuisine in an elegant setting. Known for dishes like lechon and adobo, it emphasizes quality and flavor. It's a popular choice for both casual dining and special occasions, celebrating local ingredients and culinary heritage.

We walked through the bustling streets of Makati at night to get to our nearest Aristocrat restaurant branch. Upon arrival, we were greeted by a friendly security guard and staff who showed us to our table.

Sisig is a popular Filipino dish made primarily from chopped, seasoned, and grilled or fried pork, often using the pig’s head and sometimes including the liver. The meat is typically crisped up and then mixed with onions, chili peppers, and a tangy sauce made from vinegar, calamansi (a citrus fruit), and sometimes soy sauce. The dish is often served sizzling on a hot plate, giving it a smoky aroma. It’s typically enjoyed as a pulutan (a snack or appetizer with drinks) but can also be eaten with rice as a main dish. The combination of savory, sour, and spicy flavors makes sisig a beloved and flavorful staple in Filipino cuisine.

We had a good feeling about this place. It was a chain, and we do try to avoid chains as much as possible while traveling, but it seemed wholesome.

We ordered one plate of Sisig, two garlic rice, and some Calamansi tea (Calamansi is a small citrus fruit popular in Filipino cuisine and beverages).

It tasted amazing—the pork was crispy in places, and the plate was sizzling. It was one of Jason’s favorite experiences with Sisig. It was a little expensive, but that was to be expected since we were in Makati and it was a chain restaurant.

On our way home, we found just enough room in our stomachs to try some Sisig from a street food vendor. This was only ₱85. Jason didn’t like this one as much as Erin did, though. It was three times cheaper than Aristocrat, so if you don’t mind sacrificing a bit on taste, you might enjoy this one just as much.

Manila is a great place for foodies in the Philippines, and Makati is a great area in Manila to start a fun challenge. While traveling, we like to try new food, but after a while, we tend to stick to what we know.

description:
10 Essential Tips When Visiting Istanbul, Turkey  
1. Plan Your Visit to Major Attractions
   Istanbul’s iconic sites, such as the Hagia Sophia, Topkapi Palace, and Blue Mosque, can get crowded, especially during peak tourist seasons. Arrive early or book tickets online to avoid long lines and make the most of your time.  
2. Explore Both European and Asian Sides
   Don’t limit yourself to just the European side of Istanbul. Take a ferry to the Asian side, particularly Kadiköy, to experience local markets, quieter streets, and a different cultural vibe.  
3. Use Public Transportation
   Istanbul’s public transportation system is extensive and affordable. Use the Istanbulkart, a reloadable card, for buses, trams, ferries, and metro lines. Avoid taxis during rush hours as traffic can be heavy.  
4. Dress Modestly for Religious Sites
   When visiting mosques or other religious sites, ensure your attire is modest. Women should bring a scarf to cover their hair, and both men and women should avoid shorts and sleeveless tops.  
5. Try Local Cuisine
   Indulge in Turkish delicacies like kebabs, baklava, simit, and Turkish tea. Don’t miss a traditional breakfast spread or street foods such as roasted chestnuts and stuffed mussels (midye dolma).  
6.Bargain at the Bazaars  
   The Grand Bazaar and Spice Bazaar are must-visit shopping spots. Bargaining is expected here, so negotiate politely to get a good deal on souvenirs, carpets, and spices.  
7.Take a Bosphorus Cruise 
   A Bosphorus cruise is a must-do to see Istanbul’s stunning skyline, palaces, and bridges from the water. Opt for a sunset cruise for the most magical views.  
8.Visit Neighborhoods Beyond Sultanahmet  
   While Sultanahmet is home to many of the city’s landmarks, explore vibrant neighborhoods like Balat for its colorful houses, Karaköy for its trendy cafes, and Beyoğlu for its lively nightlife and Istiklal Avenue.  
9.Respect Local Customs and Traditions
   Learn a few Turkish phrases like "Merhaba" (Hello) and "Teşekkür ederim" (Thank you). Respect prayer times in mosques and ask for permission before photographing locals.  
10. Prepare for Istanbul’s Weather
   Istanbul’s weather varies significantly by season. Bring a light jacket in spring and autumn, layer up in winter, and carry sunscreen and a hat during the summer months. Always check the forecast before heading out.  
These tips will ensure you have a smooth and memorable visit to Istanbul, a city where history and modernity blend seamlessly. About:

description:
Here are 10 important rules and facts to know when visiting the Grand Palace in Thailand:

1. Dress Code: Proper attire is required. Visitors must wear long pants or skirts and cover their shoulders. Sleeveless shirts and shorts are not allowed, so be sure to dress conservatively. This is to show respect to the cultural and religious significance of the site.

2. Opening Hours: The Grand Palace is typically open every day from 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM, but hours can vary during holidays or special events, so it’s good to check ahead.

3. Ticket Purchase*: There is an entrance fee to the Grand Palace, and tickets can only be purchased at the official ticket booths near the entrance. Avoid buying tickets from street vendors as they might be scams.

4. Respect Royalty: The Grand Palace is a royal residence and an important cultural site. Always show respect when inside, which includes not taking photos in certain areas, especially in the temples and of the royal family’s images.

5. Shoes Off: When entering temples or sacred spaces within the Grand Palace, you will be required to remove your shoes.

6. No Smoking or Vaping: Smoking is prohibited in the Grand Palace and its surrounding areas, including the gardens and temples. Vaping is also restricted.

7. Photography Restrictions: While photography is allowed in some areas, be mindful of signs that restrict photography, especially inside temples. In certain areas, flash photography and tripods are not allowed.

8. Stay Quiet: As the Grand Palace is a place of religious and cultural significance, maintain a respectful and quiet demeanor, especially when in sacred areas like the Emerald Buddha Temple.

9. Don’t Point Your Feet: In Thai culture, pointing your feet at people or religious images is considered disrespectful. Be mindful of your posture, especially when sitting or standing near sacred objects.

10. Guided Tours Available: You can hire an official guide at the entrance or use audio guides to learn more about the history and significance of the Grand Palace, as it’s filled with rich cultural heritage.

Following these guidelines will help ensure a respectful and enriching experience when visiting this iconic landmark in Bangkok! About:

description:
In today's video, we will have night walking tour in Chinatown Bangkok – one of the most exciting and flavorful places in the city. Walking along Yaowarat Road, you’ll see a mix of cultures, lights, smells, and street food like nowhere else in Bangkok. This area is famous for its street food, especially in the evening when the road comes alive with food stalls and local restaurants. 

Here are some of the most popular Thai and Chinatown dishes you can try during your visit:
Pad Thai – Stir-fried noodles with shrimp, tofu, peanuts, and a sweet-savory sauce
Hoy Tod – Crispy oyster omelette
Guay Jub – Rolled rice noodles in a peppery soup with crispy pork belly
Dim Sum – Steamed dumplings filled with pork, shrimp, or vegetables
Duck Noodles – Soft noodles with roasted duck in a rich, herbal broth.
Seafood BBQ – Grilled prawns, squid, and crab sold right on the street.
Durian – The famous “king of fruits.” Smelly, soft, sweet – and unforgettable!
Mango Sticky Rice – Sweet mango with coconut milk and sticky rice. A Thai dessert favorite.
You can also try some exotic snacks as scorpions, fried insects, silkworms and bamboo worms.

Famous Places and Restaurants:
T&K Seafood – One of the most famous street seafood restaurants in Chinatown.
Lek & Rut Seafood – Right across from T&K, another great spot for fresh grilled seafood.
Nai Ek Roll Noodles – Known for Guay Jub (peppery rolled noodle soup with pork).
Sweet Time – A dessert stall with colorful Thai sweets, including black grass jelly and coconut puddings.
Yaowarat Toast – Grilled buttery bread filled with custard or chocolate. Super popular for dessert!

Walking here, you’ll see gold shops, herbal stores, Chinese temples, and neon signs everywhere. It’s crowded, it’s loud, but it’s full of life. At night, the whole street turns into a giant open-air food market. Locals and tourists come here to eat, explore, and enjoy the energy of the city. It’s the kind of place where you try something new, take photos every few steps, and just enjoy the moment. In this video you will see Sunday night atmosphere and amazing neon lights in Bangkok. description:
In today's virtual walking tour, we will walk Bangkok's Chinatown - Best Thai and Chinese street food in Bangkok and Thailand! Bangkok’s Chinatown, known as Yaowarat, is one of the most popular areas in Thailand. It has a long history and has been a center of Chinese culture in Bangkok for more than 100 years. Today it is one of the busiest places in the city, especially at night. The main street is full of food stalls, restaurants, and shops. Visitors can try many different dishes such as noodles, roasted duck, grilled seafood, dumplings, oyster omelets, and sweet desserts. Many of these foods are famous not only in Thailand but also around the world. Chinatown is also a favorite spot for tourists and photographers. The bright neon lights, old-style buildings, and busy streets make it one of the most recognizable areas in Bangkok. At night the atmosphere is very lively, with thousands of people walking, eating, and enjoying the street markets. This area is often compared with other top attractions in Bangkok, such as the Grand Palace and Chatuchak Market. Many travelers say a visit to Chinatown is one of the highlights of their trip. In this walking tour, I will take you through the streets of Yaowarat and show you why it is considered the best place for street food in Thailand. description:
In today's virtual walking tour in Bangkok, we will visit amazing Benjakitti Forest Park - Bangkok's largest forest park. Benjakitti Forest Park is one of the most beautiful green spaces in the center of Bangkok. The park covers about 720,000 square meters (over 180 acres), making it larger than many older parks in the city. It’s Bangkok’s first forest park, combining trees, wetlands, lakes, and modern design to give a breath of fresh air in the concrete jungle. There’s a large man-made lake, fountains, and water bodies which help both with scenery and cooling the surroundings. Around the lake there are paths for running, walking, cycling — many locals come here early in the morning for exercise. One of the standout features is the elevated skywalk through parts of the park, giving panoramic views over the wetlands, the forest canopy, and Bangkok’s skyline (You can see beautiful panoramic views of Downtown Bangkok, One Bangkok Mall, All Bangkok Skyscrapers, Asok Area and etc). Wildlife is present: you can see birds, sunbirds, doves; there are also warning signs about monitor lizards, so wildlife lovers should keep their eyes open. For photography lovers, this park is a gem — especially around sunrise or sunset when the light reflects off the water and you get silhouettes of trees and the city skyline. The Green Bridge connects Benjakitti Park to nearby Lumpini Park, offering even more walking/cycling options. If you like nature, architecture, design, or just a relaxing place to hang out, this park offers all of that in one.

description:
Today we’re celebrating Happy Halloween right in the center of Bangkok — at Siam Square, the most popular place in the city for this festival. Every year this area turns into a huge Halloween street party filled with lights, music, and people in crazy costumes.

The atmosphere here is amazing. You’ll see hundreds of people dressed as zombies, ghosts, movie characters and creative cosplay looks. Everywhere you go, there’s music, dancing, and live performances. Famous Thai artists and dancers perform on big stages surrounded by spooky decorations and glowing lights.

You can walk around and watch mini horror shows, zombie parades, and funny Halloween contests. There are also many themed photo zones, decorations, and horror-movie style corners — everything looks so real and detailed.

This Halloween event at Siam Square runs from Friday to Sunday, and the most exciting part starts around 6 PM, when it gets dark and the lights come on. That’s when the whole place feels magical — the music gets louder, the crowd grows, and the real Halloween spirit begins.

Many shops and restaurants around Siam Square also join the celebration. They decorate their places with pumpkins (pumpkin head halloween), spider webs, and glowing ghosts. You can find Halloween-themed snacks, drinks, and lots of cool souvenirs.

People come here from all over Bangkok — locals, tourists, families, and students — to enjoy this night together. It’s fun, colorful, and a little scary at the same time.

If you’ve never experienced Halloween in Thailand, this is one of the best places to feel it. The mix of Thai culture and international Halloween style makes it truly special.

So join me in this video and let’s dive into the spooky streets of Bangkok together. Welcome to Bangkok Halloween at Siam Square — one of the most unforgettable nights of the year!

description:
In today's virtual walking tour, we will visit two of the best parks in Bangkok : Thailand's largest rooftop park - NEW Dusit Central Park (Dusit Arun) and Lumphini Park. First we go to Lumphini Park, a large green space in the heart of the city. The park covers about 142 acres. It’s located in the Silom–Rama 4 area and is very accessible. When you arrive you’ll see a big lake, many trees and open lawns for walking or exercising. The lake views show high-rise buildings in the background—nice mix of nature and city. One of the most unusual sights: the monitor lizards — Asian water monitor — live here. There are around 400 of them in the park (they can be quite large, often one to two metres long).The park is very old and one of the oldest parks in Bangkok (also one of the most famous parks in the city and a place many locals know). You will feel history around you when you walk there and see how the city has grown around the park.

After our time in Lumphini, we head to Dusit Central Park — the newest and largest rooftop park in Bangkok. The rooftop park officially opened for visitors on 3 September 2025. This park is part of a huge new mixed-use development at the junction of Silom and Rama 4. The rooftop green space spans 7 rai (about 11,200 m²).  It sits from the 4th to 7th floors of the complex, giving sweeping views over Lumpini Park and the city skyline. It’s designed as a relaxing green oasis, with walking trails, seating zones, and landscapes on top of the building. A lot of young people go there to hang out, walk, take photos or relax. At sunset and at night you can see the city lights and the skyline from the rooftop park — it gives incredible views. It’s just perfect: contrast between the calm of Lumphini and the modern rooftop vibe of Dusit Central Park.
